prompt: What does `@State` do for a value in a SwiftUI view?

It makes the value a global constant
It saves the value to disk
It shares the value with every view in the app
mcq.explanation: View structs are recreated often; `@State` storage is owned by SwiftUI and tied to the view's identity in the hierarchy. Keep it `private` to the view that owns it.

prompt: What does `var body: some View` mean?

mcq.explanation: `some View` is an opaque return type. Because the type is fixed, branches that return different views need `@ViewBuilder` (which wraps them in a conditional type) rather than plain `return`s.

prompt:

task.prompt:
A `ProfileView` declares `@ObservedObject var model = ProfileModel()`. Whenever its parent re-renders (for example,
a badge count changes), the profile reloads and loses the text the user was typing.

steps.question: Why does this happen?
options: `@ObservedObject` does not own the object: each time the parent re-creates `ProfileView`, a new `ProfileModel` is made
`ObservableObject` resets itself on every publish
The parent is calling `objectWillChange` on the model
steps.explanation: Observed objects are expected to be owned elsewhere. Initialising one inline gives a fresh instance with every view init.

steps.question: What is the fix (iOS 14–16 style)?
options: Declare it `@StateObject private var model = ProfileModel()` so SwiftUI creates it once per view identity
Make `model` a `static` property
Use `@EnvironmentObject` without injecting it
steps.explanation: `@StateObject` ties the object's lifetime to the view's identity, like `@State` for reference types.

steps.question: A child view `ProfileForm` needs the same model. How should it declare it?
options: `@ObservedObject var model: ProfileModel`, passed in from the parent
`@StateObject var model = ProfileModel()` again
`@State var model: ProfileModel`
steps.explanation: Only the owner uses `@StateObject`; children observe the instance they are given.

prompt: When should a view use `@StateObject` instead of `@ObservedObject` for an `ObservableObject`?

options: When the view creates and owns the object; `@ObservedObject` is for objects passed in from outside
When the object has more than one `@Published` property
Always; `@ObservedObject` is deprecated
When the object is a struct
mcq.explanation: `@StateObject` keeps a single instance for the view's lifetime. With `@ObservedObject` an inline-created object is recreated whenever the view struct is.

prompt: What is the advantage of `.task { await load() }` over `.onAppear { Task { await load() } }`?

options: The task is cancelled automatically when the view disappears, and `.task(id:)` restarts it when the id changes
It runs on a background thread automatically
It runs only once per app launch
It retries on failure
mcq.explanation: `.task` ties structured concurrency to the view's lifetime. The manual `Task` in `onAppear` keeps running after the view is gone.

task.prompt:

`DateFormatter()` inside `body`, rows are wrapped in `AnyView`, and the list is `ForEach(messages, id: \.self)` on a
`Hashable` struct whose `isRead` flag changes often.

steps.question: Why does `id: \.self` hurt here?
options: The identity includes `isRead`, so marking a message read gives it a new identity: SwiftUI destroys and recreates the row instead of updating it
`\.self` is not allowed on structs
It makes the list sort itself
steps.explanation: Identity should be stable for the lifetime of the item; use a real `id`.

options: Use a shared formatter (or `Text(date, style: .time)` / `date.formatted()`) instead of creating a `DateFormatter` per render
Move the formatter into `onAppear`
Wrap the row in another `AnyView`
steps.explanation: Formatters are expensive to create; `body` runs often.

steps.question: Why remove `AnyView`?
options: Type erasure hides the view's structure, so SwiftUI cannot diff it efficiently and rebuilds more than needed
`AnyView` does not support Dark Mode
`AnyView` is only for macOS
steps.explanation: Prefer `@ViewBuilder` and concrete types so SwiftUI keeps structural identity.

Nothing; iOS restores SwiftUI paths automatically

prompt: A view shows `if isEditing { EditForm() } else { EditForm().disabled(true) }`. Text typed into the form disappears when toggling. Why?

options: The two branches have different structural identity, so SwiftUI treats them as different views and resets their state
`disabled` clears text fields
`if` statements are not allowed in `body`
`EditForm` must be `Equatable`
mcq.explanation: Each `if`/`else` branch is a separate position in the view tree. Keep one view and vary a modifier: `EditForm().disabled(!isEditing)`.

prompt: What does adding `.id(selectedUser.id)` to a view do when `selectedUser` changes?

options: Gives the view a new explicit identity, so SwiftUI discards it (and its `@State`) and creates a fresh one
Makes the view `Identifiable`
Only changes the accessibility identifier
Nothing, unless the view is in a `List`
mcq.explanation: Changing `.id` is a deliberate reset: useful to clear a form for a new record, harmful if applied to something that changes every render.

prompt: Why mark a view model `@MainActor`?

options: All of its methods and properties run on the main actor, so UI-driving state is updated on the main thread and the compiler checks it
It makes network calls faster
It runs the model on a background thread
It is required for `Codable`
mcq.explanation: With `@MainActor`, `await`ed work can still run elsewhere, but assignments to published state happen on the main thread; calling from a background context needs `await`.

prompt: Swift 6 strict concurrency reports data races in this cache. Mark the problem lines.

task.prompt: Mark the lines that are problems.

segments.issue: A plain class with mutable state shared across tasks is not `Sendable`; make it an `actor` (or protect the dictionary with a lock).

prompt:
Memory grows each time a user opens and closes the live-scores screen. Instruments shows `ScoresModel` instances are
never deallocated. The model starts a `Timer.scheduledTimer(withTimeInterval: 5, repeats: true) { _ in self.refresh() }` in
`init` and adds a `NotificationCenter` observer with a closure that calls `self.reload()`.

task.prompt:
Memory grows each time a user opens and closes the live-scores screen. Instruments shows `ScoresModel` instances are
never deallocated. The model starts a `Timer.scheduledTimer(withTimeInterval: 5, repeats: true) { _ in self.refresh() }` in
`init` and adds a `NotificationCenter` observer with a closure that calls `self.reload()`.

steps.question: Why are the models never freed?
options: The repeating timer (held by the run loop) and the observer closure capture `self` strongly
SwiftUI keeps every view model forever
`@Published` properties leak by design
steps.explanation: The run loop retains the timer, the timer's block retains the model, so the model can never reach zero references.

steps.question: What fixes it?
options: Capture `[weak self]` in both closures and invalidate the timer / remove the observer when the screen goes away
Make `ScoresModel` a struct
Call `deinit` manually
steps.explanation: Weak captures break the cycle; invalidation stops work that would otherwise keep running.

steps.question: What is a more SwiftUI-native way to run the polling?
options: A `.task { while !Task.isCancelled { await model.refresh(); try? await Task.sleep(for: .seconds(5)) } }` on the view
A global `DispatchSourceTimer`
Polling inside `body`
steps.explanation: The task is cancelled automatically when the view disappears, so there is nothing to invalidate.

prompt: With the Observation framework (`@Observable`), which change causes a view to re-evaluate `body`?

options: A change to a property that this view's `body` actually read
Any change to any property of the model
Only changes to properties marked `@Published`
Only calls to `objectWillChange.send()`
mcq.explanation: Observation tracks property access per view. With `ObservableObject`, any `@Published` change invalidates every observing view, which is a common source of over-rendering.

prompt: A detail view uses `.task(id: productID) { await load(productID) }`. What happens when `productID` changes while a load is running?

options: The running task is cancelled and a new one starts for the new id
Both loads run and the first to finish wins
Nothing; `.task` only runs on first appearance
The view is destroyed and recreated
mcq.explanation: `task(id:)` restarts when the id changes, cancelling the old task, which avoids showing a stale product if the old request finishes last (as long as `load` checks cancellation).

prompt: Which statement about `actor` isolation is true?

options: Calls into an actor from outside are `await`ed, and an actor can be re-entered at each `await` inside its own methods, so state may change across a suspension point
Actors run all their methods on the main thread
Code inside an actor method never suspends
Actors make every property thread-safe even when accessed via `nonisolated`
mcq.explanation: Actors serialise access but are re-entrant: check or re-read state after an `await` inside an actor method instead of assuming it did not change.
